document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with two days of a painful, hot, swollen right knee. His temperature is 38.4 C, he cannot bear weight, and he holds the knee flexed. There is no history of trauma, previous joint disease, or gout, and the skin overlying the joint is intact with no cellulitis. Which investigation is most useful at this point?

options.text: Arthrocentesis for synovial fluid cell count and differential, Gram stain and culture, and crystal examination

questions.explanation: Synovial fluid analysis is done diagnostically to clarify the cause of inflammation and to differentiate inflammatory, degenerative, septic, crystal-induced, and hemorrhagic effusions. The three most important tests are the 3 Cs: culture and Gram stain, cell count and differential, and crystal examination. In an acute hot monoarthritis with fever and intact overlying skin (no absolute contraindication to aspiration), arthrocentesis is the single most informative test.

optionExplanations.b: Serum urate does not distinguish crystal arthritis from infection and cannot exclude a septic joint.
optionExplanations.c: Acute phase reactants are non-specific markers of inflammation and do not identify organisms or crystals.
optionExplanations.d: Plain films establish a baseline but do not differentiate septic, crystal, or inflammatory effusions.
optionExplanations.e: MRI is not required to characterize the joint fluid and delays the definitive test, aspiration.

questions.topic: Approach to Acute Monoarthritis and Synovial Fluid Analysis

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis on immunosuppressive therapy develops three days of fever with a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender left knee that she is unable to move. Aspiration yields turbid fluid with a white cell count of 78,000/mm3, predominantly neutrophils, and a Gram stain showing Gram-positive cocci in clusters. No crystals are seen. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Empiric intravenous antibiotics together with joint drainage and decompression
Oral antibiotics as an outpatient with review in one week
High-dose NSAIDs and observation pending final culture results
Colchicine with repeat aspiration in 48 hours

questions.explanation: Septic arthritis is a medical emergency that can cause rapid joint destruction and carries a 10-15% risk of mortality; the knee is the most commonly affected joint. Management is empiric IV antibiotic therapy (narrowed once cultures return) plus source control with joint decompression. Rheumatoid arthritis with immunosuppression and prior joint damage is a recognized risk factor, and this purulent aspirate with Gram-positive cocci confirms the diagnosis.

optionExplanations.a: Corticosteroid injection is contraindicated when sepsis is present and would worsen infection.
optionExplanations.c: Outpatient oral therapy is inadequate for a medical emergency with a 10-15% mortality risk and no source control.
optionExplanations.d: NSAIDs do not treat infection, and delaying antibiotics permits rapid joint destruction.
optionExplanations.e: Crystals were absent and colchicine does not address bacterial infection of the joint.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman reports two years of gradually worsening pain in both hands and the right knee. The pain occurs with motion and is relieved by rest, morning stiffness lasts about 15 minutes, and the knee gels after prolonged sitting. Examination shows bony enlargement of several distal and proximal interphalangeal joints, squaring of the thumb base, and crepitus on passive knee movement without warmth or erythema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis presents with insidious joint pain with motion that is relieved with rest, gelling, bony enlargement, limited range of motion, and crepitus on passive movement, with at most mild inflammation. Hand involvement characteristically affects the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes), and the carpometacarpal joint with thumb squaring, and the knee is a common site.

optionExplanations.a: Rheumatoid disease produces inflammatory synovitis with warmth and swelling, not bony enlargement with brief stiffness relieved by rest.
optionExplanations.b: Radiographic new bone formation and inflammatory features characterize psoriatic disease; there is no psoriasis or inflammatory arthritis here.
optionExplanations.d: Tophaceous gout causes episodic severely inflamed joints with urate deposits, not slowly progressive bony enlargement with crepitus.
optionExplanations.e: Lupus is a multisystem inflammatory disease; the presentation here is purely mechanical and localized to overused joints.

source.reference: RH6 — Signs and Symptoms of OA / Joint Involvement

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman has three months of pain and swelling affecting both wrists, the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands, and the metatarsophalangeal joints. Morning stiffness lasts about two hours and improves with use. She reports fatigue and weight loss. Examination shows soft tissue swelling and tenosynovitis of the affected joints, sparing of the distal interphalangeal joints, and firm subcutaneous nodules over both olecranons. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic symmetric erosive synovitis of peripheral joints (wrists, MCPs, MTPs) presenting with symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis and morning stiffness lasting more than one hour. Early physical findings include effused joints, tenosynovitis, and subcutaneous nodules as an extra-articular manifestation, exactly the pattern described here.

optionExplanations.a: Degenerative disease causes bony enlargement with brief stiffness rather than symmetric small-joint synovitis with nodules and constitutional symptoms.
optionExplanations.c: Lupus is a multisystem disease with rash, mouth ulcers, photosensitivity, serositis, or renal involvement, none of which is present.
optionExplanations.d: Psoriatic disease is usually asymmetrical, may involve the DIP joints, and is accompanied by psoriasis or nail changes.
optionExplanations.e: Gout presents with recurrent acute inflammatory attacks rather than three months of persistent symmetric synovitis with rheumatoid nodules.

source.reference: RH8 — Rheumatoid Arthritis / Features of Seropositive Arthropathies

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman is diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis after 10 weeks of symmetric synovitis of the small joints of the hands and feet with morning stiffness lasting more than one hour. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are positive. She drinks no alcohol, is not pregnant, and has normal liver enzymes, creatinine, chest radiograph, and hepatitis serology. Which is the best initial disease-modifying treatment?
questions.explanation: The key to rheumatoid arthritis management is early diagnosis and early intervention with DMARDs, started as soon as the diagnosis is made and aimed at sustained remission. Methotrexate is the gold standard and first-line agent unless contraindicated; baseline CBC, ALT, creatinine, hepatitis serology, and CXR should be checked, all of which are normal here. Response is reassessed at 3-6 months, with combination or switching if inadequate.

optionExplanations.a: NSAIDs and analgesics relieve symptoms but do not alter the course of rheumatoid arthritis.
optionExplanations.b: Low-dose prednisone is useful short-term to bridge the gap until DMARDs take effect, not as the initial disease-modifying agent.
optionExplanations.d: Biologics are indicated after an inadequate response to DMARDs and should be combined with DMARD therapy.
optionExplanations.e: Hydroxychloroquine is a weaker agent, considered when methotrexate is contraindicated.

source.reference: RH10 — Rheumatoid Arthritis: Investigations and Treatment

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman has two months of fatigue, low-grade fever, and weight loss. She describes a facial rash that flares after sun exposure, painless mouth ulcers, patchy hair loss, symmetric pain in the small joints of both hands, and pleuritic chest pain. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and red blood cells. ANA is positive. Which investigation is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This multisystem picture of photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, alopecia, polyarthralgia, pleuritis, and glomerular urinary findings should prompt consideration of SLE, which should be suspected when two or more organ systems are involved. ANA has 98% sensitivity but poor specificity and is used only as a screening test; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are the specific antibodies (95-99%), and anti-dsDNA titre with C3 and C4 is also useful for monitoring disease activity.

optionExplanations.a: Rheumatoid factor is not specific for lupus and would not confirm this multisystem presentation.
optionExplanations.c: Anti-CCP is not one of the lupus-specific antibodies; the SLE-specific serologies are anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm.
optionExplanations.d: Anti-centromere is not a lupus-specific antibody and would not confirm the diagnosis here.
optionExplanations.e: Anti-Jo-1 is not a lupus-specific antibody and does not confirm the diagnosis in this patient.

source.reference: RH12 — SLE: Clinical Presentation and Investigations

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with diffuse skin thickening of the fingers, forearms, and trunk, Raynaud phenomenon, and reflux was started on prednisone 30 mg daily three weeks ago. She now presents with severe headache and blurred vision. Blood pressure is 215/125 mmHg, urine output has fallen, creatinine has doubled, and the blood film shows fragmented red cells. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Scleroderma renal crisis occurs in 10-15% of patients with systemic sclerosis and produces malignant arterial hypertension, oliguria, rising creatinine, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. An ACE inhibitor is the treatment for this hypertensive crisis. Prednisone above about 20 mg daily may provoke renal crisis in susceptible patients, which fits the recent steroid exposure in this woman with diffuse cutaneous disease.

optionExplanations.a: Higher-dose steroids may themselves provoke renal crisis and would worsen this presentation.
optionExplanations.c: Cyclophosphamide is used for scleroderma-associated interstitial lung disease, not for renal crisis.
optionExplanations.d: Calcium channel blockers are vasodilators used for Raynaud phenomenon; they do not target the renin-driven renal crisis.
optionExplanations.e: Plasma exchange is not the treatment for scleroderma renal crisis; blood pressure control with an ACE inhibitor addresses the underlying process.

questions.topic: Systemic Sclerosis and Scleroderma Renal Crisis

source.reference: RH15 — Scleroderma: Clinical Manifestations and Treatment

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman describes three months of progressive difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, and lifting her arms to comb her hair; the weakness is painless. Examination shows a violaceous rash with oedema over both eyelids, pink-violaceous flat-topped papules over the knuckles and finger joints, and an erythematous rash across the neck, upper chest, and shoulders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies cause progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness of the shoulder and hip girdles developing over weeks to months, with difficulty arising from a chair and climbing stairs. Dermatomyositis adds characteristic skin findings: a heliotrope rash over the eyelids with oedema, Gottron's papules over the MCP and IP joints (pathognomonic, present in about 70%), and the shawl sign over neck, upper chest, and shoulders.

optionExplanations.a: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes girdle pain and stiffness rather than painless objective proximal weakness with these pathognomonic rashes.
optionExplanations.b: Fibromyalgia causes diffuse pain without true muscle weakness or characteristic cutaneous findings.
optionExplanations.c: Inclusion body myositis is slowly progressive with predominantly distal rather than proximal weakness and lacks these rashes.
optionExplanations.e: Systemic sclerosis causes skin tightening and Raynaud phenomenon, not heliotrope rash with Gottron's papules.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man has four months of nasal crusting, bloody nasal discharge, and recurrent sinusitis, followed by cough with hemoptysis. CT of the chest shows bilateral pulmonary nodules with cavitation. Creatinine has risen over two weeks, urinalysis shows proteinuria with red cell casts, and PR3-ANCA is positive. Which is the most appropriate induction treatment?

options.text: Intravenous glucocorticoids plus either cyclophosphamide or rituximab

questions.explanation: This is granulomatosis with polyangiitis: granulomatous inflammation affecting the upper airway (rhinitis, sinusitis, nasal crusting), lungs (nodules, hemorrhage), and kidneys (glomerulonephritis), highly associated with c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA. Pulmonary hemorrhage with rapidly rising creatinine is organ-threatening disease, for which induction therapy is IV glucocorticoids plus either IV or oral cyclophosphamide or rituximab.

optionExplanations.a: Glucocorticoid monotherapy is inadequate induction for organ-threatening disease, which requires an added cytotoxic or biologic agent.
optionExplanations.c: Rituximab is used as part of induction but in combination with glucocorticoids, not alone.
optionExplanations.d: Hydroxychloroquine has no role in inducing remission in ANCA-associated vasculitis.
optionExplanations.e: Antibiotics do not treat the underlying vasculitis causing the pulmonary and renal involvement.

source.reference: RH20 — Small Vessel ANCA-Associated Vasculitis: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis

questions.question: A 27-year-old man has eight months of insidious low back and alternating buttock pain. Morning stiffness lasts more than an hour, pain wakes him during the second half of the night, symptoms improve with exercise and worsen with rest, and NSAIDs taken occasionally have helped. Chest wall expansion and the modified Schober test are reduced. He had an episode of acute anterior uveitis last year. What is the best initial pharmacological treatment?
questions.explanation: Inflammatory back pain with insidious onset before age 45, morning stiffness of an hour or more, night pain worse in the second half of the night, improvement with exercise, alternating buttock pain, reduced Schober and chest expansion, and anterior uveitis indicates ankylosing spondylitis. NSAIDs are the first line of treatment for both axial and peripheral disease, alongside exercise, postural work, and physiotherapy.

optionExplanations.b: Conventional DMARDs are used only for peripheral arthritis and are not effective for axial disease.
optionExplanations.c: Sulfasalazine, like methotrexate, is reserved for peripheral joint involvement and does not treat axial disease.
optionExplanations.d: Anti-TNF or anti-IL-17 agents are considered after an inadequate response to two NSAIDs.
optionExplanations.e: Systemic steroids are only occasionally required before other effective therapy; glucocorticoids are mainly used topically or as local injections.

source.reference: RH24 — Ankylosing Spondylitis: Clinical Presentation and Treatment

questions.question: A 58-year-old man has had four attacks of acute arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint over the past 12 months, each with severe pain, erythema, and swelling resolving over about a week. A firm nodule is present over the left olecranon, and a foot radiograph shows an erosion with an overhanging edge. He is currently asymptomatic and renal function is normal. What is the best long-term management?

options.text: Intermittent NSAID courses for flares only, with no urate-lowering therapy
Allopurinol titrated to target, with low-dose colchicine prophylaxis for the first 3-6 months
Febuxostat as the first-line urate-lowering agent

questions.explanation: Recurrent podagra with a tophus over the olecranon bursa and a punched-out erosion with an overhanging edge meets the indications for urate-lowering therapy: more than two attacks per year, tophi, and bone erosions. Allopurinol is the first-line antihyperuricemic agent, started low and titrated up, and a low-dose NSAID or colchicine should be given with urate-lowering therapy for 3-6 months to avoid precipitating an acute flare.

optionExplanations.a: Treating flares alone ignores clear indications for urate-lowering therapy: frequent attacks, tophi, and erosions.
optionExplanations.b: Dietary measures are useful adjuncts but are insufficient once tophi and erosive damage are present.
optionExplanations.d: Febuxostat is second-line; allopurinol is preferred first-line and is not nephrotoxic.
optionExplanations.e: Uricosurics are used very rarely, and only in combination when a xanthine oxidase inhibitor fails to control hyperuricemia.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman reports eight months of widespread aching and stiffness, easy fatigability, and non-restorative sleep with frequent waking. She also has tension headaches and irritable bowel symptoms, and states her pain worsens with physical activity and emotional stress. There is no joint swelling and no muscle weakness; examination reveals only tenderness on palpation of soft tissues. CBC, TSH, ESR, and CRP are normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: A graded exercise programme with counselling on self-management strategies

questions.explanation: Widespread pain and stiffness with fatigue, non-restorative sleep, headaches, and irritable bowel symptoms, a soft-tissue tender examination, and normal blood work indicate fibromyalgia. Initial management is non-pharmacological: counselling on self-management strategies and graded exercise programmes including aerobic and resistance training. Pharmacological options such as low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine, or pregabalin help symptoms but are not curative.

optionExplanations.a: There is no inflammatory disease here, as reflected by the normal ESR and CRP, so steroids are not indicated.
optionExplanations.c: Opioids are not encouraged for analgesia in fibromyalgia.
optionExplanations.d: DMARD therapy treats inflammatory arthritis, which this patient does not have.
optionExplanations.e: NSAIDs are no longer encouraged in fibromyalgia and do not address sleep, fatigue, or deconditioning.

source.reference: RH30 — Fibromyalgia: Clinical Presentation and Treatment

questions.question: A 41-year-old man reports six months of pain and swelling in the right knee, the left ankle, and the distal interphalangeal joints of two fingers. Morning stiffness lasts 40 min. His nails show pitting, longitudinal ridging, and onycholysis, and the third right toe is diffusely swollen. Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale are found at the hairline and gluteal cleft. Rheumatoid factor is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis is arthritic inflammation associated with cutaneous psoriasis, which precedes the arthritis in 85% of cases, and is classified as a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. Asymmetric oligoarthritis is the most common pattern (70%), arthritis of the DIPs is characteristically accompanied by nail changes such as pitting, ridging, and onycholysis, and dactylitis with morning stiffness >30 min is typical. Hidden areas such as the hairline and gluteal cleft should be checked for psoriatic lesions.

optionExplanations.a: A symmetric polyarthritis resembling RA is one psoriatic pattern, but DIP arthritis with nail dystrophy, dactylitis, and psoriatic plaques with a negative rheumatoid factor identify psoriatic arthritis.
optionExplanations.c: Enteropathic arthritis produces large joint asymmetrical peripheral arthritis or spondylitis in the setting of ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, which this man does not have.
optionExplanations.d: Ankylosing spondylitis features symmetric sacroiliitis and axial disease rather than DIP arthritis with nail changes and skin plaques.
optionExplanations.e: Reactive arthritis follows a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection and is not associated with psoriatic plaques and psoriatic nail dystrophy.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man develops pain and swelling of the right knee and left ankle three weeks after an episode of diarrhea from which Campylobacter was cultured. He has heel pain at the Achilles insertion, a diffusely swollen second toe, bilateral conjunctivitis, and dysuria. Small shallow painless ulcers are present on the glans penis. Knee aspirate is sterile, ESR is elevated, and HLA-B27 is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Reactive arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy with peripheral arthritis and one or more extra-articular manifestations appearing shortly after a GI or GU infection, with onset 1-4 wk post-infection; Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, and C. difficile are recognized GI triggers. Asymmetric peripheral arthritis, enthesitis such as Achilles tendinitis, dactylitis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis fit the clinical triad, and balanitis circinata (small, shallow, painless ulcers of the glans penis) is diagnostic. Cultures of the joint are sterile and HLA-B27 is often positive.

optionExplanations.b: Psoriatic arthritis requires evidence of psoriasis or psoriatic nail dystrophy, neither of which is described, and it does not follow an antecedent enteric infection.
optionExplanations.c: Toronto Notes explicitly cautions that reactive arthritis should not be confused with rheumatic fever, which follows streptococcal infection and does not cause balanitis circinata or enthesitis.
optionExplanations.d: Viral arthritides are also distinguished from reactive arthritis; they do not produce keratoderma blennorrhagicum or balanitis circinata after enteric infection.
optionExplanations.e: The joint aspirate is sterile, which excludes bacterial infection of the knee.

questions.question: A 79-year-old woman describes three days of acute pain and swelling of the left wrist, with a similar self-limited episode in the right knee last year. She takes no diuretics and her serum urate is normal. Radiographs of the wrist show chondrocalcinosis. Aspiration yields cloudy fluid, and polarized light microscopy shows rhomboid-shaped crystals with positive birefringence that appear blue when aligned parallel to the compensator. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, which are rhomboid-shaped and positively birefringent (blue when parallel to the compensator), in contrast to the needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals of gout. It occurs in the elderly, is usually monoarticular in the knee or wrist, and chondrocalcinosis is the characteristic radiologic finding. Treatment of the acute attack is with NSAIDs or corticosteroids.

optionExplanations.a: Gout crystals are monosodium urate: needle-shaped and negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the compensator), and gout classically involves the first MTP with erosions showing overhanging edges.
optionExplanations.c: Hydroxyapatite is another crystal-induced arthropathy but does not produce rhomboid positively birefringent crystals with chondrocalcinosis.
optionExplanations.d: Osteoarthritis is degenerative and does not produce an acute crystal-positive inflammatory effusion.
optionExplanations.e: An infected joint would show organisms rather than crystals, and chondrocalcinosis with positively birefringent crystals identifies calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman describes three years of daily gritty dry eyes and a dry mouth that makes her drink liquids to swallow dry food. She has several new dental caries and angular cheilitis. Schirmer's test is 3 mm/5 min in each eye and anti-SSA/Ro is positive. Artificial tears, humidifiers, hydration, and good dental hygiene have improved her eyes but not her xerostomia. What is the most appropriate treatment for her persistent dry mouth?
questions.explanation: Sjogren's syndrome is characterized by dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) from lymphocytic infiltration of the salivary and lacrimal glands, and this woman meets classification criteria with a positive anti-SSA/Ro and a Schirmer's test of 5 mm/5 min or less. For xerostomia refractory to hydration and dental hygiene, parasympathomimetic agents that stimulate salivary flow, such as pilocarpine, are the appropriate next treatment.

optionExplanations.b: Systemic treatments such as hydroxychloroquine are ineffective for the sicca symptoms of Sjogren's syndrome.
optionExplanations.c: Corticosteroids are likewise ineffective for sicca manifestations and add unnecessary toxicity.
optionExplanations.d: Rituximab is reserved for severe organ-threatening disease such as vasculitis, not for isolated dry mouth.
optionExplanations.e: Topical nystatin or clotrimazole for 4-6 wk treats oral candidiasis, which is not described here, and does not restore salivary flow.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman has three weeks of new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, and pain in the muscles of mastication on prolonged chewing, together with shoulder and pelvic girdle stiffness. This morning she developed sudden painless loss of vision in the right eye. The temporal artery is tender on examination, ESR is 92 mm/h, and CRP is 68 mg/L. Colour Doppler ultrasound and temporal artery biopsy are booked for tomorrow. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily for 3 d followed by high-dose prednisone 1 mg/kg/d PO in divided doses with taper
Prednisone 1 mg/kg PO in divided doses started only once the temporal artery biopsy is reported
Withhold glucocorticoids and repeat ESR and CRP after the ultrasound
Low-dose ASA with analgesia while awaiting biopsy

questions.explanation: Giant cell arteritis must be treated on clinical suspicion because untreated disease causes permanent blindness in 20-25% of patients. When a patient presents with vision loss at diagnosis, treatment is methylprednisolone 1000 mg/d IV for 3 d followed by high-dose prednisone 1 mg/kg/d PO in divided doses with taper. This woman is over 50 with new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms, and a markedly elevated ESR and CRP.

optionExplanations.b: Steroids must be started immediately on clinical suspicion; waiting for a biopsy risks permanent blindness, and biopsy yield is not lost by starting treatment promptly.
optionExplanations.c: Deferring glucocorticoids for further testing in a patient who already has vision loss risks irreversible bilateral blindness.
optionExplanations.d: Low-dose ASA is only an adjunct considered when there is critical involvement of the vertebral or carotid arteries and does not treat the arteritis.
optionExplanations.e: Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, is used in combination with glucocorticoids for new or relapsing disease, not as sole emergency therapy for vision loss.

source.reference: RH22 — Large Vessel Vasculitis: Giant Cell Arteritis

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman of Asian descent has six months of fever, weight loss, and fatigue. Examination shows unequal peripheral pulses: blood pressure is 146/88 mmHg in the right arm and unobtainable in the left, with an absent left radial pulse. Investigations show anemia and an elevated CRP; there is no evidence of infection or malignancy. Angiography shows inflammatory thickening of the aorta and its branches. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The source classifies Takayasu's arteritis as a large vessel vasculitis - "pulseless disease" with unequal peripheral pulses and chronic inflammation, most often of the aorta and its branches, and most common in young adults of Asian descent aged 10-40 with F>M predominance. Vasculitis is suspected in systemic illness with constitutional symptoms and no evidence of malignancy or infection, with non-specific labs such as anemia and increased CRP, and angiography is the investigation when tissue is inaccessible. This young woman's absent left radial pulse, unequal arm blood pressures, and inflamed aorta and branches fit that description.

optionExplanations.b: Giant cell arteritis also involves the aorta and its branches but occurs at age 50 or older and presents with temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and vision loss.
optionExplanations.c: Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium vessel segmental, non-granulomatous necrotizing inflammation with average age 40-50 and M>F, not large vessel disease with unequal pulses.
optionExplanations.d: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small vessel ANCA-associated vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract and kidneys causing sinusitis, pulmonary hemorrhage, and glomerulonephritis.
optionExplanations.e: Microscopic polyangiitis is a pauci-immune necrotizing small vessel vasculitis affecting kidneys, lungs, and skin, and is most common in older age.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman has six weeks of aching pain and stiffness in her neck, both shoulder girdles, and both hip girdles, with fever, malaise, and weight loss. She has prolonged morning stiffness of about 60 min duration. Examination shows tender muscles but no true weakness or atrophy. Blood work shows anemia of chronic disease, elevated platelets, elevated ESR and CRP, and a normal CK. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bilateral subdeltoid bursitis with biceps tenosynovitis

questions.explanation: The source describes polymyalgia rheumatica as pain and stiffness of the symmetrical proximal muscles of the neck, shoulder and hip girdles with prominent constitutional symptoms, prolonged morning stiffness, and no muscle weakness; the required criteria are age 50 yr or more, bilateral shoulder aching, and abnormal ESR/CRP, with additional points for morning stiffness of 45 min or more, hip pain, absence of RF or ACPA, and absence of other joint involvement. Blood work in polymyalgia rheumatica often shows anemia of chronic disease, elevated platelets, elevated ESR and CRP, and a normal CK, and physical exam reveals tender muscles but no true weakness or atrophy. This woman meets the required criteria and shows exactly that pattern of girdle pain, prolonged morning stiffness, and tender muscles without weakness.

optionExplanations.b: Fibromyalgia is chronic widespread non-articular pain with characteristic tender points; it does not produce fever, weight loss, anemia of chronic disease, or elevated ESR and CRP.
optionExplanations.c: Polymyositis causes true proximal muscle weakness with an elevated CK, whereas this patient has tender muscles with no weakness or atrophy and a normal CK.
optionExplanations.d: Giant cell arteritis is commonly associated with polymyalgia rheumatica but is suggested by headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness, none of which are present.
optionExplanations.e: Subdeltoid bursitis and biceps tenosynovitis are localized periarticular soft tissue disorders and do not explain symmetrical neck, shoulder and hip girdle involvement with prominent constitutional symptoms.
